description: Portable processor scenarios for the OpenAPI 3.1 binding-specification sibling. Configuration is named semantically; adapters normalize HTTP observations.

scenarios.description: A later patch-looking OpenAPI edition is refused at load instead of accepted by version-line inference.
Same-named path and query parameters remain independently writable through the qualified parameter-key mode inside the caller envelope. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

Two concrete request-media entries preserve both declared alternatives, but the sole-concrete rule requires configuration.requestMedia before a required body can consume input; examples and supplied value shape select neither.
An operation with no concrete success-response media omits Accept instead of inventing application/json.
A 201 response uses the default declaration for response media/decode but remains successful because classification is independently 2xx.
The same default declaration may describe a 404 body but never upgrades that non-2xx status into success.

Several effective servers require explicit `server` selection; array order does not create an OpenBindings default. With that consumer choice missing, invocation is context-required before dispatch and nothing reaches the wire.
An omitted optional header parameter emits no destination, so the selected credential with the same declared destination emits once and dispatches.
An API-key credential targeting processor-owned Accept cannot replace response-media negotiation and is refused before dispatch.

A request-body schema reached through $ref and allOf is resolved before media handling; the envelope's body member carries the complete application value. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A media type declared for a different success status cannot govern the actual response.

A parameter name and a body-property name occupy disjoint envelope members; the explicit requestMedia choice selects the safe media candidate without losing the independently supplied header parameter, and the supplied body does not elect. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An OAS header parameter named Authorization is ignored by the artifact's own rule: it creates neither a required input nor a wire header.

Two OAS-distinct header parameters that differ only by case collide on HTTP's case-insensitive field channel, exclude the selected target, and refuse before dispatch. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

Two content-map keys that differ textually but denote the same parsed media type are a normalized collision; with no usable sibling, request selection refuses before dispatch rather than selecting the first key. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A response media declaration with matching parameters outranks its unparameterized sibling while additional actual parameters remain admissible.
Two distinct response declarations tying at the greatest matching parameter specificity are a protocol error rather than content-map order precedence.
A 303 response is not followed by rewriting the artifact-bound POST to GET; it remains the final non-2xx failure response. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An application object whose own members resemble the former private routing tuple remains ordinary data inside the envelope's body member. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A location-backed multi-document description resolves an external Path Item and Security Scheme, and fragment-only Parameter, Request Body, and Response references inside the external document stay scoped to that document. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
Security Requirement Objects are alternatives: when two complete alternatives are available, an explicit security choice selects exactly one and never unions their credentials onto the wire.
Credentials are never volunteered when the effective operation declares no security requirement.
Raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations coexist, but an invocation supplying values that make both channels emit refuses before dispatch.
An effective Host header parameter cannot replace processor-owned target resolution and is refused before dispatch even when omitted by the caller.
An effective Content-Length header parameter cannot replace processor-owned body framing and is refused before dispatch even when omitted by the caller.
An OAS 3.1 schema-omitted image body uses the OpenBindings Base64 boundary and emits raw bytes. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An OAS 3.1 contentEncoding string is transferred as encoded text and is not decoded as OpenBindings boundary Base64. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A required range-only object body challenges for requestMedia during preflight before input consumption and performs zero dispatch; object shape does not imply JSON. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A configured application/json concrete type instantiates a wildcard declaration while the envelope body remains the pure application value. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An exact media declaration outranks type and universal ranges for a configured concrete request media type. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A type range outranks a universal range for a configured concrete request media type. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A configured concrete media type covered by a range still refuses when the first candidate defines no encoder for that governing schema and media combination. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
A configured text/plain concrete type covered by a wildcard refuses when the governing schema and supplied value are objects. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
An optional range-only request body with no caller value bypasses media selection and emits neither a body nor Content-Type.

An optional range-only body supplied without prior requestMedia refuses after input is present rather than issuing an unsafe replay challenge. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]
The actual concrete response media selects an OAS 3.1 range, whose schema-omitted body preserves exact bytes as Base64.
A concrete application/json response selected through application/* still emits the parsed JSON application value.

An OAS 3.1 pattern property selects the effective schema and application/json default for a dynamic multipart member inside the envelope's body value. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A declaration-complex exact JSON request remains the envelope's one body value; binding correspondence never selects a schema branch or body field. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A single-non-null-branch choice part carries its branch's serialization. This scenario also asserted, until 2026-08-17, that an unconstrained part beside it takes its OAS per-type default from the value's JSON application type — at `openapi: 3.1.2`, whose Encoding Object default table states application/octet-stream for a part whose `type` is absent. That half was wrong and moved to OAPI30-PS-56 and OAPI31-PS-57, which carry the type-absent cell per line. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A urlencoded property whose Encoding Object declares none of style, explode or allowReserved takes the OAS's content-based path, which the OAS pairs with RFC 1866 Section 8.2.1; a space therefore rides as +. The OAS also records that percent-encoding it as %20 satisfies the media type, so both spellings are permitted observations and neither is this specification's preference. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: RFC 1866 Section 8.2.1: space characters are replaced by +.
OAS 3.1.2 Section 4.8.12.4 records that %20 also meets the media type's requirements.

scenarios.description: The same property with an Encoding Object declaring style takes the OAS's style-based path, which the OAS pairs with RFC 6570 and notes "does not use + for form-urlencoded"; a space therefore rides as %20. The two paths spelling a space differently is incorporation, not divergence. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: RFC 6570 expansion percent-encodes the space, and the OAS states of this path that it "does not use + for form-urlencoded". One permitted observation, not a set.

scenarios.description: Path selection inside an urlencoded body is by an Encoding Object field's explicit PRESENCE, not by its value. OAS 3.0.4/3.1.1/3.1.2 say "the presence of at least one of style, explode, or allowReserved with an explicit value is equivalent to using schema with in: \"query\" Parameter Objects", and OAS 3.1.0 says of each field "If a value is explicitly defined, then the value of contentType (implicit or explicit) SHALL be ignored." allowReserved: false restates the field's own default, so it is an explicit value and takes the style path. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: Explicit presence of allowReserved: false selects the style path, so SPACE serializes as %20 rather than the content path's + spelling.

scenarios.description: An array-valued multipart property takes its per-part default Content-Type from its ITEMS schema, never from the array. Every accepted OAS edition states this, in one of two ways. The Encoding Object's contentType default says "for array – the default is defined based on the inner type" (3.0.0–3.0.3, 3.1.0), "according to the type and format of the items schema" (3.0.4), "according to the type of the items schema" (3.1.1, 3.1.2). Independently, the multipart guidance in 3.0.0–3.0.3 and 3.1.0 says "If the property is a primitive, or an array of primitive values, the default Content-Type is text/plain". A string items schema with no contentEncoding therefore reaches text/plain on every edition, and each element takes its own part. An engine that keyed the default on the array itself would emit ONE part carrying the whole JSON array, which is what the per-element body assertions below exclude. The per-part Content-Type header is deliberately NOT asserted: [RFC7578] Section 4.4, which 3.1.1 incorporates, says "Each part MAY have an (optional) 'Content-Type' header field, which defaults to 'text/plain'", so emitting it and omitting it are both inside the permitted set and requiring either would invent a preference the authority does not state. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: Two parts named tags, each carrying one item as its whole body. An array-keyed default would put ["alpha","beta"] in one part and match neither body assertion.

scenarios.description: Every accepted OAS 3.1 edition states application/octet-stream as the default contentType for a part whose `type` is absent — 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 in the first row of the Encoding Object's own default table, 3.1.0 through the total catch-all that closes its prose enumeration. The authority therefore routes the part to octets, and openbindings.openapi-3.1@1 carries them across the JSON seam with the canonical Base64 boundary it already defines for every other byte lane: the part is emitted under that default content type with the decoded octets as its body. This scenario pinned a pre-dispatch refusal until 2026-08-20, on the ground that no JSON-to-octet part boundary existed; the boundary did exist, and the revision-is-not-a-roadmap ruling directed the gap filled rather than deferred, applying an existing boundary to a cell the authority had already routed. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A multipart property declared as an array, supplied a value that is not an array, refuses before dispatch. §9.2 says of the form-serialization lanes that "An invalid value or a member for which the resolved schema leaves no faithful form carriage refuses before dispatch." The declaration is what decides this part's carriage — an array property rides as one part per element, which OAPI31-PS-55 pins — so a value carrying no elements has no faithful form carriage at all. The failure mode this excludes is silent: a processor that falls back to the WHOLE-property schema serializes the invalid value into one application/json part, the artifact's own declaration never described that part, and the caller is told nothing. Refusing is also the only outcome that keeps the two lanes agreeing, since the same processor refuses the declaration outright when the declared schema leaves no carriage. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

expected.description: No request is emitted. A processor keying the part on the whole-property schema instead would dispatch one application/json part carrying "alpha".

scenarios.description: A multipart part whose resolved Schema Object declares a non-string type and also carries `contentEncoding` keeps its own per-type default row. Every accepted 3.1 edition keys the application/octet-stream row on a declared string — 3.1.0 as "a `type: string` with a `contentEncoding`", 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 as the Encoding Object default table's `string` row with contentEncoding present — while the `number, integer, or boolean` row holds `n/a` in the contentEncoding column, which that table's own note defines as "the presence or value of contentEncoding is irrelevant". The incorporated dialect says the same independently: JSON Schema 2020-12 makes the Content vocabulary annotations that "do not function as validation assertions" and conditions both `contentEncoding` and `contentMediaType` on the instance being a string. So an integer part carrying `contentEncoding` rides as text/plain carrying the value's own text, and does not take the encoded-string row, an octet boundary this revision does not define, or a refusal no edition states. The `sample` part's own Content-Type header is deliberately not asserted: a text/plain part may carry the header explicitly or omit it, and [RFC7578] Section 4.4 makes both the same wire fact — the reason OAPI31-PS-55 declines the same assertion. What IS asserted is that the part carries the value's own text rather than an encoded-string or octet body, and that the sibling `note` part, which declares `type: string` with the same `contentEncoding`, still takes the encoded-string row and remains artifact-encoded text while emitting no Content-Transfer-Encoding field. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

info.title: Inert content keywords on a declared non-string part

scenarios.description: Absent input with a required non-path parameter REFUSES before dispatch: OAS makes `required` mean the parameter is mandatory, and every document of this family incorporates that reading — an invocation omitting a mandatory parameter is not an invocation of the operation the artifact describes. Minimality-audit M9 briefly removed this refusal on implementation grounds; the removal was reversed as drift on 2026-09-01 (ruling R2), the specification authorities prevailing over shipped behavior.

A supplied empty caller envelope that has no body member where requestBody.required is true refuses before dispatch exactly like absent input: the required-body refusal's ground is the artifact's own requestBody.required, and §9.1 applies it to absent and supplied-but-incomplete input alike. The twin of OAPI30-PS-31 on the supplied side of the one rule. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

An explicit unevaluatedProperties: false remains a 3.1 schema assertion, but CO31-03 deletes declaration-complex correspondence: the envelope body directly carries the complete application value. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

A normalized collision CONFINES to the colliding parsed identity: the two application/json spellings are unusable, but the map's non-colliding application/vnd.safe+json sibling is still an ordinary selectable alternative and dispatches under its own declaration. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

The other half of confinement, on the same artifact: no request selection may LAND on the colliding parsed identity. Configuring it refuses before dispatch instead of picking one of the two colliding spellings by source order. [CO31-03: caller input re-keyed to {parameters?, body?}.]

Response-side confinement: a normalized collision between two application/json spellings does not poison the map's clean text/plain declaration, which still governs the decode and is advertised in Accept.
The other half on the response side, same artifact: no response match may be GOVERNED BY the colliding parsed identity. A peer selecting it is a protocol error rather than a first-key decode.
An unknown caller-envelope top-level key refuses before dispatch; only parameters and body are admitted.
A present non-object parameters member refuses before dispatch.
An unknown key inside the parameters member refuses before dispatch.
A cross-location name collision activates qualified mode for every parameter, so the bare name refuses before dispatch.
A well-formed caller envelope supplies colliding path and query parameters through their qualified keys and dispatches successfully.

A root jsonSchemaDialect other than the incorporated OpenAPI 3.1 base dialect excludes the whole source at source scope, including schema-free targets. The selector reaches no admitted source and therefore refuses at resolution; this is not a defect-derived source refusal.
An effective Parameter Object declaring both schema and content is upstream-invalid and removes the target before caller values are inspected.
A supplied JSON number on a schema-form parameter refuses when parameterConversion is not configured; the binding defines no canonical fallback.
A whole null value in the form query cell serializes as the corrected undefined bytes name=.
A null array member has no RFC 6570 list representation and refuses before dispatch.
A deepObject member value containing its structural ampersand delimiter refuses instead of percent-encoding the ambiguity.
The unified resolved-declaration proof follows $ref and allOf and excludes a form-style object member that declares only an object compound shape.
An effective path Parameter with no corresponding template expression is upstream-invalid and removes the selected target as invalid.
Two templated path keys with the same static hierarchy are upstream-invalid and remove either selected target as invalid.
A schema-form Header Parameter value containing CR/LF refuses before an HTTP field is constructed.
Raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations alone exclude nothing; supplying only the raw Header Parameter emits exactly that Cookie field.
An optional 3.1 form-style cookie array remains represented, and omitting it dispatches without a Cookie field.
A typeless exploded cookie declaration survives static proof, but a supplied array that actually produces multiple pairs refuses at invocation time.
A path-template expression with no corresponding effective path Parameter is upstream-invalid and removes the selected target as invalid.
OAS 3.1 does not forbid a path-template expression from occurring more than once. Its one effective path Parameter supplies the same value at every occurrence.
A completed target whose operation path contains a malformed percent escape cannot parse and percent-decode under RFC 3986 and refuses before dispatch.

A caller-supplied request Content-Encoding is admitted by the effective Header Parameter, but runtime encoder capability does not support its token. The condition is never skipped or sniffed: a request-side condition refuses before dispatch.

Content-coding implementations are runtime capabilities, not binding configuration points. The actual Content-Encoding field fixes the coding stack even when the governing Response Object declares no Header Object for it. An absent declaration therefore imposes no content-coding constraint and does not declare identity; the runtime decoder removes the coding before the selected media lane.
A governing non-Content-Type response Header Object declaring required true makes the actual header mandatory; absence is a loud response protocol error even for an empty body.
A non-empty response without Content-Type assumes application/octet-stream before ordinary declaration matching and crosses the raw boundary as canonical Base64.
A non-empty actual response with no governing Response Object is a loud protocol error; another status declaration cannot govern it.
A text/event-stream response remains unary under this binding: one HTTP body produces one application string rather than a predecessor streaming sequence.
The actual request and response Content-Encoding fields name identity, which needs no runtime codec: both stacks preserve the representation bytes unchanged.
readOnly and writeOnly are application annotations: the binding preserves both supplied JSON members on the request wire instead of deleting either one.
A supplied nullable property on the content-based form-urlencoded path is elided as an omitted optional member and contributes no field.
An explicit Encoding style selects the RFC 6570 path, where a supplied nullable primitive follows the corrected form-style undefined cell and emits name= instead of being blanket-elided.

The usable-set election floor: after the normalized collision makes both application/json spellings unusable, application/vnd.safe+json is the map's exactly-one USABLE concrete alternative and self-selects with no requestMedia configuration, per the amended sole-concrete gloss (exactly one usable entry self-selects; supplied values never elect). [Pins the ratified usable-set election ruling.]

A consumer-supplied Server Variable value outside the declaration's nonempty enum refuses before dispatch; a complete configured URL is the distinct replacement lane, not permission to weaken the selected Server Object.

A declaration-derived query-bearing Server alternative is upstream-invalid at that smallest owner; with no sibling or configured recovery, the represented target refuses while awaiting configuration.server The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A declaration-derived fragment-bearing Server alternative is upstream-invalid at that smallest owner; with no sibling or configured recovery, the represented target refuses while awaiting configuration.server The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A complete configured HTTPS URL recovers a target whose sole declaration-derived Server alternative is unusable, while leaving method, path, parameters, body, response, and security semantics unchanged.
Two complete security alternatives require an explicit configuration.security choice even when runtime credentials could satisfy both; artifact order creates no preference and nothing dispatches.
An effective empty security array is a complete no-security alternative: it self-selects, dispatches, and never volunteers unrelated runtime credential material.
A query apiKey comes only from runtime credential context, never the caller envelope, and every reserved, space, and non-ASCII UTF-8 byte is percent-encoded under Section 8.2.
An apiKey cookie value containing a semicolon is not an RFC 6265 cookie-value; it refuses before dispatch and is never percent-encoded into an invented recovery.
A credential/header-parameter collision makes only that security alternative unusable; explicitly selecting the non-colliding alternative emits only its credential and dispatches.
Raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations alone exclude nothing: when the invocation supplies only the structured cookie parameter, the operation completes and emits that cookie.
With the same raw-Cookie and structured-cookie declarations, supplying both values refuses before dispatch rather than parsing or merging the raw Cookie string.
Strict-JSON response parsing resolves duplicate object member names by taking the lexically last member, inside RFC 8259 Section 4's permitted receiver set.
Omitting the required response description is documentary coverage loss only; the valid sibling content declaration still governs and decodes the successful JSON response.

Basic user-id and password octets are pinned to printable US-ASCII; a non-ASCII credential is not a usable credential, so the invocation completes context-required instead of electing an RFC 7617-undefined encoding.

A leading byte-order mark on a JSON response body is ignored under RFC 8259 Section 8.1's parser latitude and is never part of the value: the body parses to exactly the value that follows the mark, and the mark leaves no trace in any decoded string.

A lone surrogate escape in a JSON response body yields no value: it is a loud protocol error after a 2xx final status, because neither silent replacement of the escape nor invalid-Unicode passthrough preserves the supplied text. No partial unary value is emitted.

Compound-capable style admission reads the resolved declaration: in an anyOf whose only branch not declaring solely null is an array of strings, that branch is the single resolved member declaration, so spaceDelimited stays admitted and the query carries the OAS Style Examples bytes.
A supplied header parameter value is carried as UTF-8 octets: U+00E9 goes on the wire as C3 A9, not as the single Latin-1 octet E9.

An admitted exact key whose value is not a Response Object retains precedence and remains an invalid response alternative, but it does not remove the target; an empty successful response dispatches and completes with no output.
A non-map response headers member is confined to that invalid projection and imposes no constraint; the valid sibling content declaration still governs and decodes the successful JSON response.
A non-Header response member is confined to that projection while a valid required header sibling still governs; one actual X-Good field satisfies it and the JSON body decodes.
A response defect confined to one target does not affect a sibling operation in the same source; selecting the intact sibling still resolves, dispatches, and completes.

A defect in a Response Object that can never govern a 2xx — here an exact 404 — does not remove the target, because failure data is best-effort. The target whose success path is intact still resolves and dispatches; synthesis separately accounts the invalid 404 Response projection as coverage loss.

A selector naming a method the Path Item does not declare reaches no addressable target: the selector does not resolve and the invocation REFUSES AT RESOLUTION, the outcome §3.2's vocabulary added for this case. Nothing reaches the wire.

A selector whose escaped path segment names no Paths Object key likewise reaches no addressable target and refuses at resolution. The Paths Object is non-empty, so this is selector non-resolution and not a source refusal.

The negative control for the two scenarios above, and the discrimination §3.2's vocabulary creates: a selector naming a target removed as INVALID still resolves. The Parameter Object omits its required `name`, which §8.1 makes an upstream-invalid declaration removing the selected target; §3.2's removed-unit rule then says the selector naming it still resolves and the invocation refuses BEFORE DISPATCH. Same absent dispatch, different phase from OAPI31-PS-130 and OAPI31-PS-131.

A Schema Object `default` is never inserted by this binding: an unsupplied optional query parameter carrying one is omitted before serialization exactly as one carrying none, so the completed URL carries only the supplied parameter. The governing text draws the distinction while defining the Server Variable Object's own `default` — "Note that this behavior is different from the Schema Object's `default` keyword, which documents the receiver's behavior rather than inserting the value into the data" — and an engine that inserted it would emit flavor=vanilla beside size=large.

The same rule on the header channel: an unsupplied optional header parameter carrying a Schema Object `default` emits no field at all. Asserted as an absent header rather than an empty one, because the rule omits the parameter before serialization rather than serializing the default.

A body-emitting invocation emits a request `Content-Type` carrying the elected media type in its PARSED form: type, subtype, and parameter name lowercased, and the parameter value in the characters the declaration supplied after unquoting. The sole declaration key is spelled `Application/JSON;Charset="UTF-8"`, so an engine echoing the key would emit the uppercase spelling and an engine normalizing the VALUE too would emit charset=utf-8. The delimiter between type and parameter is deliberately not asserted: §9.1 fixes the case of each token and the quoting of each value, and states no spelling for the separator, so `contains` pins exactly what the document fixes and no more.

Which spelling matched never changes the emitted bytes: a range-keyed declaration instantiated by a mixed-case `requestMedia` choice emits the choice's media type in parsed form, lowercased. The declaration key contributes no spelling of its own here, so the emitted value can only come from the choice, and only through the normalization §9.1 pins.

§9.1's parameter-value comparison pin, charset half: a declared media-type parameter value is unquoted first, and the value of `charset` then compares ASCII case-insensitively. Two usable entries force a `requestMedia` choice; the choice spells charset=UTF-8 against a declaration spelling charset=utf-8 and MUST still match, electing the JSON lane. The emitted parameter's case is deliberately not asserted — §9.1 says the value is emitted "in the characters the declaration or choice supplied" and the two differ here, so the document fixes no answer.

§9.1's parameter-value comparison pin, boundary half: every parameter value other than `charset`, `boundary` included, compares by EXACT character sequence, because RFC 2046 Section 5.1.1 constructs the multipart boundary delimiter from the value literally and an inexact boundary does not delimit. The choice spells boundary=ABC against a declaration spelling boundary=abc, matches no entry, and refuses before dispatch. OAPI31-PS-139 is the positive control proving the multipart entry is otherwise usable.

The positive control for OAPI31-PS-138, and the testable half of §9.3's declared-boundary rule: a `boundary` carried by a declaration key takes part in §9.1's matching, and an exactly-spelled choice elects the multipart alternative. The emission half — that the declared token is then discarded and the processor's generated token is emitted in its place — is NOT asserted here: §9.3 declares the generated token free, and this scenario format has no negative or pattern assertion able to state that the declared token is absent.

A supplied request value at a raw-octet boundary that is a JSON string containing a non-alphabet character refuses before dispatch: no non-alphabet character is skipped and the decode is never partially applied. RFC 4648 Section 3.3 requires rejecting encoded data containing characters outside the base alphabet unless the referring specification states otherwise, and §9.2 states no such exception.

The same boundary refuses a JSON string whose padding is missing: §9.2 requires padding and states that no repair supplies it. `QQ` is the unpadded spelling of the canonical `QQ==`, and an engine that tolerated it would dispatch a single 0x41 octet the caller never wrote in canonical form.

The same boundary refuses a JSON string with non-zero unused pad bits, the last of §9.2's four canonicality conditions. `QR==` carries one octet in two symbols, and RFC 4648 Section 3.5 requires the four unused bits of the second symbol to be zero; `R` is value 17, whose low four bits are 0001. Both `QQ==` and `QR==` decode to 0x41 under a tolerant decoder, which is exactly the non-canonicality Section 3.5 describes.

The first limb of the same rule: a supplied request value at a raw-octet boundary that is not a JSON string at all refuses before dispatch. Every OpenBindings raw-octet value is a JSON string, so a supplied number reaches no decode.

The `or part` half of the same rule: the refusal is at the affected body OR PART. The `profile` part declares no type, so §9.3 routes it to the raw-octet lane and §9.2's canonical Base64 boundary — the carriage OAPI31-PS-57 pins for a well-formed value — and a non-canonical string there refuses the whole invocation before dispatch rather than emitting a partly-decoded part.

§9.3's incorporated multipart entity framing, in the two respects this format can state. Each part's `name` parameter is emitted as a quoted-string, the pinned spelling of the two RFC 9110 Section 5.6.6 calls equivalent. And each part's content is followed by CRLF and the two hyphens that open the next delimiter, which holds at both the inter-part position and the closing position; only CRLF represents a line break between body parts, so an engine emitting a bare LF anywhere in that seam fails both content assertions. Cross-property part order is declared free by §9.3, and both assertions hold under either order.

A response whose single `Content-Type` field value is a list of media types selects NO media type. RFC 9110 Section 8.3 defines the field as a single media-type and defines no resolution for the list shape, and its application/octet-stream assumption is granted for an ABSENT field and does not reach a present one. On a successful response that is a loud protocol error, not a first-member or most-specific decode: the declaration would match application/json on either picking rule, so an engine that picked would emit a value here.

The unsuccessful half of the same rule, and the half that distinguishes it from an ordinary protocol error: on a response the classification does not admit as successful, no governing content declaration matches, so §9.5's best-effort failure-body rule yields NO failure-data value and raises no loud protocol error. The declaration would decode this body cleanly if the field named one media type — OAPI31-PS-07 is that scenario, and it carries the decoded body as failure data — so an absent failure-data value here is the whole observable difference the list-valued field makes.

§8.2's exclusion tests the WHOLE Style Examples row. The spaceDelimited/explode:true row is n/a in all four of its columns — undefined, string, array, and object — so the combination is excluded whatever the caller supplies, and the target refuses before dispatch. The supplied array would serialize under the sibling explode:false row, which OAPI31-PS-123 pins, so an engine reading the row as merely the array cell of some other row would dispatch here.

The other side of the whole-row test: a row carrying n/a in SOME columns and real bytes in others is a supported combination, and a value falling in a real column serializes. The spaceDelimited/explode:false row is n/a for undefined and string and real for array and object; OAPI31-PS-123 pins its array column, and this pins its object column against the shape of the OAS Style Examples cell `color=R%20100%20G%20200%20B%20150` — the object member name and its value alternate, joined by the percent-encoded delimiter. One member is supplied deliberately: neither §8.2 nor the Style Examples fixes the ORDER in which the members of one object value are written, so a multi-member assertion would pin bytes this specification does not state.

info.title: Supported column of a mixed row

scenarios.description: §8.2's own named instance of the whole-row test: an omitted `explode` on `deepObject` computes to false, whose entire row the edition leaves undefined, so the parameter is excluded and the target refuses before dispatch. The supplied object would serialize under the explode:true row that OAPI31-PS-85 exercises, so the defaulting is the whole of what is under test here.

§9.3's Encoding media-type selection governs BOTH content-based lanes, not multipart alone: the edition places `contentType` among the Encoding Object fields that "MAY be used either with or without the RFC6570-style serialization fields" and attaches the multipart-only restriction to `headers` instead. The `note` property is a plain string, whose default cell is text/plain and would ride as note=hello; an explicit Encoding contentType of application/json routes it through §9.2's JSON lane instead, so the field carries the JSON text "hello" percent-encoded. The Encoding Object declares no style, explode, or allowReserved, which is what selects the content-based path.

info.title: Encoding contentType on the form lane

scenarios.description: An unquoted numeric Responses key loads and the operation completes. YAML's Core schema resolves the plain scalar 200 to tag:yaml.org,2002:int, but an OpenAPI document is itself a JSON object that YAML merely represents, so the key is the JSON member name it spells. This is the ordinary OpenAPI YAML idiom.

source.content:
openapi: 3.1.2
info:
  title: T
  version: '1'
servers:
  - url: https://api.example
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        204:
          description: ok

scenarios.description: A plain scalar key never refuses on its resolved type, whichever Core-schema tag that resolution assigns: an unquoted true in key position is the member name it spells, and the document loads.

servers:

x-vendor:

paths:

scenarios.description: What refuses at the key gate is a key that is no scalar at all. A sequence in key position is no representation of a JSON member name and refuses at load.

The invoke half of the unsatisfiable-property accounting: the part `bad` admits no instance, so it is not a routed field, and a value supplied for it fails every admission test and refuses before dispatch at that part (Section 5.2). No request is emitted. A processor that dropped the value silently and dispatched the remaining parts would be sending a request the caller did not describe; one that excluded the target at synthesis would have removed an operation on a defect nothing reaches (the companion synthesis scenario pins that half).

expected.description: No request is emitted: the supplied `bad` value reaches a part no value can satisfy.

scenarios.description: A supplied empty string for a query Parameter that declares no allowEmptyValue serializes as the form row's empty cell, q=: the edition's Style Examples define the empty string's bytes independently of allowEmptyValue, and the empty string is not undefined.

A body-free invocation of a `trace` target whose Operation declares an optional `requestBody` dispatches with method TRACE, no body, and no Content-Type field. Section 7: the binding emits no body on `trace`, because a TRACE client MUST NOT send content (RFC 9110 Section 9.3.8), and Content-Type indicates the media type of the associated representation (RFC 9110 Section 8.3), so a request carrying no representation carries no such field. The same wire fact is pinned on every 3.x sibling. Whether a runtime's platform HTTP API can send TRACE at all is a host limit outside this specification: a runtime that cannot refuses before dispatch, and never dispatches another method in its place.

A required request body with two usable concrete media alternatives and no requestMedia choice is context-required before dispatch. The portable scenario asserts only the binding-specification outcome; target, durability, and challenge-record layout belong to an invocation interface's own conformance suite.

A 3.1 content-based form property whose propertyMedia choice selects application/json carries the supplied array as its JSON image with a configured parameterConversion never consulted: Section 8.1 scopes the converter to schema-form parameter serialization and the RFC 6570-style Encoding path, never for Section 9.3's content-based path, which Section 9.3 serializes by media type.

A 3.1 content-based form property whose explicit single concrete Encoding contentType is application/json carries a supplied integer and boolean as their JSON images with a configured parameterConversion never consulted: Section 8.1 names the converter never for Section 9.3's content-based path, which Section 9.3 serializes by media type.

A body-free invocation of a `trace` target whose Operation declares a `required: true` requestBody dispatches with method TRACE, no body, and no Content-Type field, the required-declaration companion of OAPI31-PS-157. Section 7: on such a content-forbidding method the artifact's `required: true` request body creates no caller-body requirement, so a body-free invocation dispatches and the preceding `incorporated` rule's missing-required-body refusal does not reach it; the target is therefore invocable, not permanently unusable. The ground is RFC 9110 Section 9.3.8: a client MUST NOT send content in a TRACE request, so no declaration can oblige the caller to supply one. OAPI32-PS-35 pins the same cell on 3.2. The declaration is reported as coverage loss at the Request Body position, a synthesis observation outside this processor scenario's assertions. Whether a runtime's platform HTTP API can send TRACE at all is a host limit outside this specification: a runtime that cannot refuses before dispatch, and never dispatches another method in its place.

info.title: TRACE with a required body declaration

scenarios.description: Appended is pinned here to one and only one seam repair: the implied root server and the Paths key are joined by removing only their redundant seam slash. A Paths key beginning // therefore retains its intentional doubled slash, distinguishing the narrow join from both verbatim concatenation and broad slash normalization.

A text lane whose type decision encounters $dynamicRef is excluded at that media alternative because the binding does not perform JSON Schema dynamic-scope evaluation; a supplied string cannot turn the reference into a static walk.
A required Request Body Object with an empty content map leaves no candidate media type, so the addressable target is excluded and invocation refuses before dispatch.
A required nullable content-based form property cannot be represented by elision; supplying null refuses before dispatch instead of silently producing the same wire form as omission.
A fixed name-based Content-Disposition value naming another property contradicts OAS's mandatory property-to-part mapping, so the multipart alternative is excluded before dispatch.
An API-key security alternative whose declared header destination is not an HTTP token is excluded before any credential value is inspected.
A 204 response cannot carry content. Even when the governing Response Object declares text content, actual response bytes are a loud protocol error and are never decoded into an output value.
A non-token optional ordinary Header Parameter is excluded only at that projection; omitting it leaves the operation dispatchable.
The would-be caller key of an excluded optional non-token Header Parameter is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required ordinary Header Parameter excludes its addressable target, whose invocation refuses before dispatch.
An ordinary Header Parameter cannot give the caller control of Transfer-Encoding; the addressable target is excluded and refuses before dispatch.
A 101 response is an immediate loud response-phase protocol error because this unary binding has no upgraded-protocol continuation; the processor does not wait for another HTTP response.

A non-HTTP artifact Server does not destroy the addressable or represented operation, but the artifact-derived completed target refuses before dispatch. The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.
A complete configured HTTPS URL replaces a non-HTTP artifact Server and dispatches the otherwise unchanged operation.
A non-token optional cookie Parameter is excluded only at that projection; omitting it leaves the operation dispatchable.
The would-be caller key of an excluded optional non-token cookie Parameter is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required cookie Parameter excludes its addressable target, whose invocation refuses before dispatch.
A non-token required response Header Object key excludes its response alternative; a successful response governed by it is a loud response-phase protocol error.
A content-form cookie Parameter whose exact serialized value is not an RFC 6265 cookie-value refuses before dispatch; the binding neither escapes nor repairs it.
A default-only Responses Object is valid, and its fallback Response Object governs an otherwise unmatched successful status.
A leading SP is field-line whitespace rather than part of an RFC 9110 field-value, so an ordinary Header Parameter cannot preserve it and refuses before dispatch.
A raw Cookie Header Parameter must serialize to a complete RFC 6265 cookie-string; a value without a cookie-pair refuses before dispatch.
A header apiKey credential ending in HTAB is not an RFC 9110 field-value and refuses before dispatch.
A selected header apiKey named Cookie is a raw Cookie source; combining it with a supplied structured cookie Parameter refuses before dispatch.
A selected header apiKey named Cookie and a selected cookie apiKey in the same AND requirement are raw and structured Cookie sources; combining them refuses before dispatch.
ASCII-case variants denote one response field: one received field discharges the group and the complete Content-Encoding value satisfies every binding-understood finite constraint.
Case-equivalent required Encoding headers with conflicting exact artifact values exclude the multipart alternative rather than selecting a key by case or map order.
An omitted optional parameter creates no collision; the selected credential emits once and dispatches.
A supplied optional parameter and selected credential that reach the same actual field refuse before dispatch.
An exploded runtime object is not statically excluded, but its actual serialized token destination collides with the selected query credential and refuses before dispatch.
A required ordinary Proxy-Authorization parameter is excluded at the target boundary because that field authenticates to the first inbound proxy, not the origin API.
Ordinary and credential query contributions form one unordered multiset while preserving each contribution's encoded bytes.
An anonymous TRACE alternative survives and dispatches without volunteered credential fields.
A TRACE target whose sole alternative emits a credential refuses before dispatch.
A generated multipart name uses UTF-8, emits qdtext literally, and escapes only DQUOTE and backslash with one quoted-pair.
A followed cross-origin redirect strips binding-selected header credentials and does not append the original query credential to the Location target.
Supplying request Content-Encoding on an invocation that emits no request representation refuses before dispatch.
A case-insensitive HTTP bearer scheme consumes one valid b64token and constructs the exact Authorization field.
A valid OAuth2 Bearer token uses the same exact RFC 6750 Authorization construction.
A valid OpenID Connect Bearer token uses the same exact RFC 6750 Authorization construction.
An empty HTTP bearer credential cannot satisfy b64token and refuses before dispatch.
A space inside an OAuth2 access token is outside b64token and refuses before dispatch.
CR/LF in an OpenID Connect token is outside b64token and refuses before dispatch without emitting a field.
An explicitly non-Bearer OAuth2 runtime token has no carriage under this identifier and refuses before dispatch.

HEAD carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. The installed Brotli decoder fails if called, so successful empty completion proves the method-based no-content rule does not invoke it.

A 304 response carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. A failing Brotli sentinel is installed, but the no-content rule does not invoke it. Because 304 is not successful, completion remains the native unsuccessful response.

A non-UTF-8 character request lane requires its direction-specific encoder. With no such runtime capability, encoding refuses before dispatch rather than being reported as a response error or silently substituted.

On a successful HEAD response, resolving the Header schema $ref and filtering the mixed enum yields the exact domain containing only identity. The wire value 7 therefore fails; ignoring the reference or stringifying the numeric enum member would incorrectly complete.

A Server Variable Object missing its REQUIRED default is upstream-invalid at the Server alternative. With no surviving declaration-derived alternative or configured recovery, invocation refuses before dispatch. The same represented target can proceed with a conforming complete URL, so this missing context is the context-required refusal species.

A successful HEAD response still validates Content-Encoding field grammar before the no-content rule suppresses decoding; a non-token coding-list member fails loudly even though no decoder is invoked.
A successful HEAD response still applies its governing exact raw-string Content-Encoding domain; gzip is outside the declared br domain and fails loudly without invoking a content decoder.

Request and response character codecs are independent directional capabilities. The request encoder is installed and permits dispatch, while the response decoder is a failing sentinel and therefore produces a loud response-phase error.

A successful HEAD response evaluates nested allOf constraints recursively. The outer domain admits identity or br, but the nested exact domain admits only identity, so br fails; a shallow implementation would incorrectly complete.
A URL expression without a matching Server Variable declaration is not excluded, but an invocation that supplies no exact substitution is context-required on configuration.server.
An exact consumer substitution completes a URL expression even when the Server Object has no matching Server Variable declaration.

A 204 response carries a syntactically valid, declaration-admitted Content-Encoding field but no content octets. The installed Brotli decoder fails if called, so successful empty completion proves the status-based no-content rule does not invoke it.

Case-equivalent response Header declarations govern conjunctively rather than by first-key selection. The first identity domain admits the actual field, but the second br domain rejects it, so the response fails loudly.

Case-equivalent response Header declarations govern conjunctively rather than by last-key selection. The first br domain rejects the actual field, although the second identity domain admits it, so the response fails loudly.

A caller-supplied JSON request value containing one unpaired surrogate code unit refuses before dispatch. The corpus materializes U+D800 after parsing its JSON-safe template so neither U+FFFD replacement nor an emitted lone-surrogate escape can masquerade as the supplied value.

An excluded optional non-token header projection sharing its declared name with a surviving query parameter is removed before caller-key uniqueness is computed; the surviving query parameter therefore uses its unqualified key and dispatches.
Because the removed header projection does not activate qualified mode, the would-be qualified query key is unknown input and refuses before dispatch.

Every admitted response-content media alternative is advertised once at equal preference in deterministic normalized order, while a case-insensitive q parameter is confined to its excluded alternative and cannot become an Accept weight.
A generated multipart Content-Disposition carries the declared part name and invents neither filename nor filename*.
An admissible artifact-fixed Content-Disposition may carry a literal filename and is emitted verbatim rather than replaced or derived from the supplied value.
An artifact-fixed multipart Content-Disposition containing filename* excludes that media alternative under RFC 7578 and refuses before dispatch when it is the only required request lane.
A present caller-envelope value that is not a JSON object is outside the closed envelope grammar and refuses before dispatch; it is never treated as a body value or parameter map.
An optional exploded form-cookie array remains represented, and a supplied one-item value emits exactly one Cookie pair.
A required non-exploded form-cookie array remains represented, and a supplied one-item value emits one valid Cookie pair.
A typeless non-exploded form-cookie declaration survives static analysis, but a supplied array reaches OAS 3.1's unsupported multi-value Cookie representation and refuses.
A nested runtime object under a typeless deepObject member leaves the admitted scalar-member cell and refuses without private stringification.
A required Request Body whose sole object-model XML alternative is excluded has no surviving effective request-content alternative and excludes the target.
Accept advertises admitted media from both success and failure Responses, but a failure-only problem media type cannot govern an actual 200 response.
A required exploded form-cookie object remains represented, and a supplied one-property value emits exactly one Cookie pair under that property's name.
A supplied empty array is present rather than omitted and uses the form undefined-value cell, emitting one empty Cookie pair rather than disappearing or entering the multi-value refusal path.
